content: Efforts to enhance early childhood development emphasize the importance of nurturing care, which includes promoting health, nutrition, safety, security, responsive caregiving, and opportunities for early learning. A structured framework has been developed to guide parents and caregivers in providing this nurturing care to young children. The World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF have established global strategies to support infant and young child feeding, including breastfeeding promotion in maternity and newborn care facilities. Growth monitoring, when combined with growth promotion activities such as nutrition counseling, has been shown to be more effective than growth monitoring alone. However, there is limited information on the integration of breastfeeding and complementary feeding counseling during immunization visits, with studies indicating missed opportunities to provide these services. For example, a study in Bangladesh revealed that while 88% of children under two years of age were seen by health workers for immunizations, only 8% of mothers reported receiving breastfeeding or complementary feeding information during these visits. Similarly, in Italy, vaccination visits were used to assess breastfeeding rates, uncovering lower rates than national and global recommendations. In Tasmania, Australia, a pilot study evaluated the feasibility of collecting infant feeding data during vaccination visits, finding that while brief discussions on infant feeding were possible, these visits were not suitable for extensive breastfeeding support due to time constraints. Growth monitoring should be linked with nutrition counseling on feeding practices and growth promotion. While brief, targeted messages about breastfeeding benefits can be communicated during immunization visits, more comprehensive counseling may require referrals to dedicated infant feeding consultations. Waiting times at immunization clinics could also be utilized to reinforce key health messages, including those on nutrition and breastfeeding. Vitamin A supplementation is critical for supporting rapid growth and combating infections during childhood. Deficiency in vitamin A can lead to visual impairment and increased risk of illness and death from infections such as measles and diarrhea. Many countries have successfully integrated vitamin A supplementation into routine health visits and immunization services. For example, in Sierra Leone, vitamin A supplementation was effectively delivered alongside routine immunizations and child health services, achieving high coverage rates. Long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) are another key intervention, particularly in malaria-endemic regions. WHO recommends universal coverage of LLINs, with distribution through antenatal and child immunization services. However, operational challenges such as stockouts, logistical issues, and inadequate training of health workers can hinder effective distribution. Joint planning for training, logistics, and data collection is essential for successful implementation. Intermittent preventive treatment in infancy (IPTi) with antimalarials has been developed to leverage the protective effects of chemoprevention against malaria. Administered during routine immunization visits, IPTi has been shown to be cost-effective in areas with moderate to high malaria transmission. In summary, integrating nutrition, malaria prevention, and other health interventions into routine immunization services offers significant opportunities to improve child health outcomes.
